corrections.corrects: the seven rows the capture recorded as 'clean, no work' with disposition 'resumed'. The STATE was true; the DISPOSITION word was wrong.
corrections.truth: Those worktrees really were clean at 13:55Z, but the instances working them were never actually stopped. The lanes kept writing after the capture, and each lane's continuation was launched as a NEW agent rather than as a continuation of the instance that already held the checkout — so TWO instances of one lane ran per checkout, and they collided. Three lanes hit it and each diagnosed it independently: p154-conflict (a live peer in the engine and vocab worktrees, _inbox/2026-09-14_p154-conflict_worker-collision.md), p156-bastrop (a superseded instance that found the writer already at work over the declaration and stood down, _inbox/2026-09-14_p156-bastrop_superseded-instance_report.json), p183-querypoint (a duplicate describe block, duplicated test helpers and a mid-flight `UU` conflict on nodeFacetBakeTier1ConformantCli.ts, _inbox/2026-09-14_p183-querypoint_collision_c964d973.json).
corrections.why: The same point-in-time defect as C1, one layer up. C1 was a WORKTREE read as a stop state; C2 is a set of WORKERS read as stopped when they were still live. 'Stopped' and 'resumed' are different acts, and the capture verified the first without performing it. A capture proves what a worktree holds at T; it proves nothing about whether its writer has quit.
corrections.handling: Every colliding instance applied the fan-model rule (one lane, one checkout, one writer) without being told: each stood down, wrote a machine-readable collision note instead of the lane's CP2/close, removed only the artifacts it had itself introduced, and deferred the canonical close to the owning instance. No lane close was written twice and no work was lost. The p183 clean-up worked: its duplicate block and helpers were removed and the project typechecks at 0 errors.
corrections.notFixedHere: The planner did NOT retro-stop anything or reassign a lane by hand. The surviving writer in each checkout was already the right one, and reaching into a lane's checkout to tidy a record is how work gets lost. The defect is recorded, not papered over.
corrections.forM0: Launching a continuation while the original may still be live is a duplication hazard; the safe form is to confirm the original is quiescent (its own 'I am stopping' artifact) before a replacement is dispatched, and to prefer continuing the SAME instance where the harness supports it.

The dispatch is kept as the record of one that was correctly not sent.

corrections.corrects: the planner's own method — the common root of C1, C2 and C3
corrections.truth: All three corrections are ONE defect: a point-in-time reading reported as a settled state. C1 — a worktree read at 13:55Z and reported as the stop state. C2 — seven workers assumed stopped because their worktrees were clean. C3 — two worktrees captured as unowned at 08:43 and reported as unowned work while their owner was merely between operations and finished it by 08:53. In each case the reading was accurate when taken and wrong within minutes, and in each case the planner's NEXT action (a resume, a dispatch) would have created a duplicate writer.
corrections.why: Three corrections to its own record in one session is the signature of a method problem, not three separate slips. A capture is a photograph; a lane's state is a moving thing.
corrections.handling: The rule that would have caught all three: before any resume or dispatch, RE-READ the worktree AND confirm the writer is quiescent, and treat a clean worktree as evidence about FILES rather than about PEOPLE. The planner did apply it once, at the moment it mattered most — it checked PR #401 and the LDT worktree immediately before dispatching the p154-surfaces lane, found the work already done, and retired the dispatch unsent (C3).
corrections.forM0: Proposed lesson: 'A worktree read is evidence about files, not about people. Never conclude a worker has stopped from a clean worktree, a quiet process list, or a prior capture; wait for the worker's own stopping artifact, or re-read at the moment of acting, before touching its territory.'

openItems.question: The probe SUPPRESSES failures instead of reporting them when a record point is absent. `runLegs` computes `const pt = legs.facets.recordPoint` and then hands `{ measured: false, error: "no record point; point leg not attempted" }` to THREE legs — `envelopeByPoint`, `gisRing` and `footprintNear`. An unmeasured leg does not fail a row. So for P-175, whose entire subject IS the record point, a parcel with NO point at all produces fewer measured legs and can read greener than a parcel with a wrong point (which does fail: the probe self-tests 'P-175 FAILS when a record point is present but 35 miles away', line 865). The absent point is the defect and it is the one shape the instrument cannot fail on.
openItems.handling: Recorded, not fixed: the planner is not the probe's owner and amending an instrument mid-wave would invalidate every artifact this wave cites. It is written down because it bounds what this wave's P-175 readings can be claimed to prove: they prove a WRONG point fails; they do not prove an ABSENT point fails. The lane's own words are the accurate framing — 'a leg-suppression, not an honest measurement'.
openItems.owner: the wave that owns scripts/surface-probe.mjs, before P-175 is used as a graduation predicate again
